learningPath.objective: Locate failures by layer and design secure, observable network paths.
topics: packet capture, socket state, DNS/TLS/HTTP tracing, and path tests
latency budgets, bandwidth-delay product, queueing, bufferbloat, and capacity
firewalls, zero trust, mTLS, DDoS controls, SSRF, request smuggling, and egress
multi-region routing, anycast, service discovery, meshes, and failure domains

theorySections.title: Layering, forwarding, and MTU
theorySections.explanation: Each hop forwards a network-layer packet using a routing decision while link-layer frames are rebuilt for the next local medium. Encapsulation adds headers and reduces payload space. If a path cannot carry a packet, IPv4 may fragment under limited conditions, while robust endpoints use path-MTU discovery and avoid black holes caused by blocked ICMP feedback.
keyPoints: MAC addresses are local-link identifiers; IP addresses support routed delivery.
Switches learn source MAC locations; routers choose next hops by longest-prefix match.
TTL/hop limit prevents indefinite routing loops.
MTU, MSS, tunneling overhead, and ICMP handling affect seemingly random large-request failures.

theorySections.title: IP addressing, subnetting, routing, and NAT
theorySections.explanation: CIDR represents an address prefix whose length determines network and host portions. Routers select the most specific matching route, then resolve the next-hop link address. NAT rewrites address/port mappings and creates state that affects inbound reachability, failover, and observability; it conserves or translates addressing but is not a security model by itself.
keyPoints: Subnet size follows 2^(address bits − prefix length), subject to protocol/reservation context.
Default gateway is simply the next hop for routes not more specifically matched.
Longest-prefix match beats route listing order.
Stateful NAT can expire idle mappings and complicate protocols carrying addresses.

theorySections.title: TCP reliability, flow, and congestion
theorySections.explanation: TCP provides an ordered byte stream using sequence numbers, acknowledgements, retransmission, and connection state. Receiver windows protect the receiver; congestion control protects the network by adapting the sending rate to loss and delay signals. TCP preserves order, so loss can delay later bytes even when they arrived, and application message boundaries must be framed separately.
keyPoints: The three-way handshake synchronizes sequence state and confirms bidirectional reachability.
Flow control and congestion control solve different bottlenecks.
One send does not correspond to one receive; TCP is a byte stream.
TIME_WAIT protects old segments and permits reliable close; it is not automatically a leak.

theorySections.title: DNS resolution and caching
theorySections.explanation: A stub resolver typically asks a recursive resolver, which follows cached or authoritative referrals through the DNS hierarchy. Records carry TTLs, and negative answers may also be cached. DNS can succeed differently across clients due to cache state, split-horizon views, search paths, record families, load-balancing policy, and DNSSEC validation.
keyPoints: Recursive and authoritative servers have different responsibilities.
CNAME aliases names; it does not redirect HTTP or preserve a URL path.
Changing a record does not instantly purge existing caches.
A/AAAA reachability, resolver choice, and Happy Eyeballs can change observed behavior.

theorySections.title: TLS identity and key establishment
theorySections.explanation: TLS negotiates protocol parameters, authenticates the server through a certificate chain and hostname verification, establishes fresh session keys through key agreement, and protects later records for confidentiality and integrity. Encryption without correct certificate validation can still connect securely to the wrong peer; TLS does not validate application authorization or sanitize content.
keyPoints: The certificate binds identities to a public key through a trusted chain and policy.
SNI selects a virtual host; ALPN negotiates an application protocol such as h2.
Forward secrecy limits retrospective decryption when long-term keys later leak.
mTLS authenticates clients at the transport layer but still needs authorization policy.

theorySections.title: HTTP versions, intermediaries, and caching
theorySections.explanation: HTTP defines methods, status codes, headers, representation metadata, and cache semantics independent of a specific transport mapping. HTTP/1.1 commonly pipelines poorly across connections, HTTP/2 multiplexes streams over one TCP connection but still shares transport loss, and HTTP/3 maps streams over QUIC to reduce cross-stream head-of-line blocking. Proxies and CDNs can transform, cache, retry, and route requests, so end-to-end behavior must include them.
keyPoints: Safe and idempotent are semantic properties, not synonyms.
Cache-Control, validators, Vary, and shared/private scope jointly determine caching.
A 502/503/504 often identifies an intermediary failure class, not the root cause by itself.
Retrying non-idempotent work requires an application idempotency design.

misconceptions.claim: A switch uses IP addresses and a router uses MAC addresses.
misconceptions.correction: A switch primarily forwards local frames by MAC; a router selects an IP next hop and then uses the local link mechanism, often MAC, for that hop.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Layer responsibilities are taught as mutually exclusive device labels instead of one packet path.

misconceptions.claim: TCP guarantees that one send becomes one receive.
misconceptions.correction: TCP preserves an ordered byte stream and can split or coalesce writes arbitrarily; applications need framing.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Small local tests often happen to preserve apparent message boundaries.

misconceptions.claim: UDP is always faster than TCP.
misconceptions.correction: UDP has less built-in machinery, but an application needing reliability, congestion control, ordering, or handshake security must implement comparable work.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Header size is compared while complete application requirements are omitted.

misconceptions.claim: HTTPS means the website is trustworthy and safe.
misconceptions.correction: TLS authenticates a hostname/key relationship and protects transport; the endpoint may still be malicious or vulnerable.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Browser lock indicators are interpreted as content endorsement.

misconceptions.claim: DNS propagation has a fixed global duration.
misconceptions.correction: Caches expire according to TTL and resolver behavior; authoritative changes are visible as individual cached entries refresh.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Distributed cache expiry is simplified into a single propagation event.

misconceptions.claim: HTTP 502, 503, and 504 are equivalent server errors.
misconceptions.correction: They distinguish bad upstream response, temporary unavailability, and upstream timeout in an intermediary context, guiding different checks.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: All are grouped as retryable 5xx without tracing the proxy path.

revisionChecklist: Trace encapsulation from application bytes to frames and back at each hop.
Calculate IPv4 CIDR ranges and apply longest-prefix routing.
Explain ARP/neighbor discovery, NAT state, ICMP, MTU, MSS, and path-MTU discovery.
Compare UDP and TCP by required semantics rather than speed slogans.
Trace TCP handshake, byte stream, retransmission, flow control, congestion control, teardown, and TIME_WAIT.
Resolve a hostname through stub, recursive, root/TLD/authoritative servers, caches, TTL, CNAME, A/AAAA, and DNSSEC context.
Trace TLS 1.3 identity, certificate verification, key agreement, SNI, ALPN, resumption, and mTLS.
Compare HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, and HTTP/3 plus caching and idempotency semantics.
Explain L4/L7 proxies, load balancing, CDNs, WebSockets, gRPC, retries, draining, and health checks.
Debug with ip/route/ss/dig/curl/openssl/tcpdump using hypotheses by layer.
setup: Record interface addresses, prefixes, routes, resolver configuration, proxy variables, and active VPN/container namespaces.
Install or identify ip/ifconfig, route, ss/netstat, dig/nslookup, curl, openssl, traceroute, and a packet-capture tool.
Use a disposable client/server pair so connection states, partial reads, timeouts, and retries can be reproduced safely.
Capture clocks and correlation identifiers across client, proxy, load balancer, and server before diagnosing latency.
Know where TLS keys, trust stores, firewall policy, load-balancer health, DNS zones, and CDN cache rules are managed.
runtime: An application resolves a name, selects an address, opens a socket, and asks the OS transport stack to exchange bytes or datagrams.
The host chooses a route, resolves the local next-hop link address, encapsulates a packet in a frame, and hands it to an interface.
Routers decrement hop limit, apply forwarding/policy/NAT as configured, and rebuild link framing for the next hop.
TCP or QUIC manages connection state, loss, flow, congestion, and cryptographic/application negotiation as applicable.
Proxies, load balancers, CDNs, service meshes, and origins each add independent timeout, retry, cache, and failure behavior.
testing: Test protocol framing with split/coalesced reads, truncation, duplicate delivery, reordering where allowed, and malformed lengths.
Test DNS changes under cache, multiple A/AAAA results, failure, and resolver differences.
Test TLS expiry, hostname mismatch, missing intermediates, client-certificate policy, and rotation overlap.
Use fault injection for latency, loss, resets, partial responses, proxy retries, backend draining, and regional failure.
debugging: Localize the failure by layer: name resolution, route/neighbor, transport socket, TLS identity/negotiation, HTTP semantics, intermediary, or application.
Compare client timestamps with server and intermediary traces; a client timeout alone does not reveal where time was spent.
Inspect socket states and retransmission/zero-window signals before assuming application CPU is slow.
Capture the narrowest safe packet sample and account for offload, encryption, NAT, and asymmetric paths when interpreting it.
performance: Decompose latency into DNS, connect, TLS, request queue, server, first byte, transfer, and client processing.
Relate throughput to bandwidth-delay product, congestion window, receiver window, loss, and number of independent connections/streams.
Reuse connections and sessions where safe, but bound pools and respect backend capacity and load-balancer draining.
Control retry amplification with budgets, jitter, deadlines, idempotency, and backpressure across every intermediary.
security: Verify certificate chains and hostnames; encryption without intended-peer authentication is insufficient.
Restrict ingress and egress by identity and destination, protect metadata/internal endpoints from SSRF, and validate proxy headers at trusted boundaries.
Harden HTTP parsing across intermediaries to prevent request smuggling and normalize ambiguous framing.
Use DDoS rate/connection controls, mTLS where appropriate, short-lived credentials, and observable policy decisions.
failureModes: A wrong route, prefix, neighbor entry, or MTU black hole makes only some destinations or payload sizes fail.
DNS caches, split-horizon views, stale negative answers, or IPv6/IPv4 differences produce client-specific behavior.
TCP retransmission, zero windows, connection-pool exhaustion, or TIME_WAIT port pressure is mistaken for an application bug.
Certificate hostname/chain/time problems or SNI/ALPN mismatch breaks TLS despite IP reachability.
Independent proxy/backend timeouts and retries amplify load or duplicate non-idempotent work.
Load-balancer health checks pass while the real dependency path, tenant data, or expensive endpoint is unavailable.

workedExamples.title: Frame messages over a TCP byte stream
workedExamples.explanation: A four-byte network-order length frames one message. recv loops because TCP may return fewer bytes than requested, and EOF before the declared length is an incomplete frame.

workedExamples.title: Inspect DNS, TCP/TLS, and HTTP separately
workedExamples.code:
dig api.example.com A AAAA
openssl s_client -connect api.example.com:443 -servername api.example.com -alpn h2
curl --resolve api.example.com:443:203.0.113.10 -v --http2 https://api.example.com/health
workedExamples.explanation: The commands isolate naming, certificate/protocol negotiation, and an HTTP request to a chosen address. --resolve preserves the hostname for SNI and certificate verification while bypassing ordinary DNS selection.

workedExamples.title: Retry an ambiguous request with an idempotency key
workedExamples.code:
POST /payments
Idempotency-Key: 6f1d...stable-per-business-attempt

transaction {
  existing = idempotency_results.find_for_update(key)
  if (existing) return existing.response
  payment = ledger.capture(command)
  idempotency_results.insert(key, hash(command), payment.response)
  return payment.response
}
workedExamples.explanation: The key is stable across retries and stored atomically with the business result. Concurrent duplicates return the recorded response, while reuse with a different request hash is rejected.

questions.prompt: A laptop sends to an IP outside its subnet. Whose MAC address goes in the Ethernet frame?
questions.answer: The destination IP remains the remote host, but the local Ethernet destination is the next-hop default gateway's MAC, learned through ARP or neighbor discovery. Each router removes and rebuilds the link-layer frame for its next hop.
questions.whyTricky: Candidates assume the remote server's MAC travels end to end.
rubric: Names the gateway MAC.
Keeps the remote destination IP.
Explains per-hop frame replacement.

questions.prompt: Why is TCP a byte stream rather than a message protocol?
questions.answer: TCP numbers and delivers ordered bytes; send calls only place bytes into the stream, and segmentation, buffering, retransmission, and receive sizes are independent. Applications must frame messages using lengths, delimiters with escaping, or a structured protocol.
questions.whyTricky: Local send/receive tests frequently align buffers and create a false message-boundary guarantee.
rubric: States no message boundaries.
Explains split/coalesce behavior.
Provides a correct framing method.

questions.prompt: Differentiate flow control from congestion control.
questions.answer: Flow control uses receiver-advertised capacity to avoid overrunning the endpoint. Congestion control estimates safe load for the network path and adjusts the congestion window based on acknowledgements, loss, and delay. Effective in-flight data is constrained by both.
questions.whyTricky: Both reduce sender rate and use window-like values.
rubric: Identifies receiver versus network constraint.
Names advertised and congestion windows.
Explains their joint limit.

questions.prompt: Trace opening https://example.com from an empty cache.
questions.answer: Resolve DNS through configured recursive infrastructure, choose an address, route/neighbor-resolve the first hop, establish TCP or QUIC, perform TLS with SNI, certificate/hostname verification and ALPN, send an HTTP request, traverse proxies/CDNs/origin as configured, receive/cache the response, then fetch dependent resources under connection and cache policies.
questions.whyTricky: Answers usually omit one of naming, local forwarding, identity verification, protocol negotiation, or intermediaries.
rubric: Covers DNS and local/routed forwarding.
Covers transport plus TLS identity/ALPN.
Covers HTTP/intermediary/cache behavior.

questions.prompt: Why can ping succeed while HTTPS fails?
questions.answer: ICMP reachability tests a different protocol and policy. TCP/443 may be filtered, no listener may exist, routing may be asymmetric, DNS may choose another address, TLS may fail identity/protocol negotiation, or an HTTP proxy/backend may fail. Test layer by layer with route, socket, TLS, and HTTP evidence.
questions.whyTricky: Reachability is treated as proof that every higher-layer dependency works.
rubric: Separates ICMP from TCP/TLS/HTTP.
Names multiple layer-specific causes.
Uses layered diagnostic commands.

questions.prompt: Explain TIME_WAIT and when many TIME_WAIT sockets are a problem.
questions.answer: The active closer retains state long enough to absorb delayed duplicate segments and retransmit the final acknowledgement, protecting a later connection with the same tuple. Many entries can be normal at high connection churn; they matter when ephemeral ports or state capacity exhaust. Prefer pooling/keepalive and correct ownership before unsafe timeout tuning.
questions.whyTricky: The visible socket count is mistaken for leaked live connections.
rubric: Explains duplicate/final-ACK purpose.
Identifies active closer and tuple reuse.
Diagnoses actual resource exhaustion before tuning.

questions.prompt: HTTP request timed out after a retry and created two payments. Which layer is responsible?
questions.answer: A timeout is ambiguous: the first request may have committed while its response was lost. Transport or proxy retries cannot infer application outcome. The payment API needs a stable idempotency key, atomic key-to-result storage with the business transaction, duplicate/concurrent request handling, and safe replay of the recorded result.
questions.whyTricky: At-least-once delivery and lost responses are mistaken for failed execution.
rubric: Recognizes ambiguous outcome.
Places idempotency at the application/business boundary.
Requires atomic persistence and replay semantics.

questions.prompt: Compare HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 head-of-line blocking.
questions.answer: HTTP/2 multiplexes streams but uses one ordered TCP byte stream, so a lost TCP segment delays delivery of later bytes across all streams. HTTP/3 uses QUIC stream-level ordering over UDP; loss in one stream does not block delivery of data in another, though congestion control and connection-level limits are still shared.
questions.whyTricky: Both protocols advertise multiplexing, which is confused with identical loss behavior.
rubric: Explains TCP connection-level ordering.
Explains QUIC per-stream delivery.
Notes remaining shared connection constraints.

flashcards.back: Choose the routing entry with the most specific matching network prefix.
Resolve a local IPv4 next-hop address to its link-layer address; it does not find remote-host MACs across routers.
Reliable ordered byte stream; applications define message framing.
Receiver capacity versus network-path capacity.
Aliases one DNS name to another; it is not an HTTP redirect.
Validate chain, time/policy, and hostname; encryption alone does not authenticate the intended peer.
Repeating the same intended request has the same intended effect, though responses and incidental logging may differ.
QUIC gives independent ordered streams, reducing cross-stream transport head-of-line blocking.

technologies.title: Computer Architecture

learningPath.objective: Use Computer Architecture idiomatically in tested application code.

theorySections.title: Core abstraction
theorySections.explanation: Computer Architecture turns informal behavior into explicit models whose assumptions, invariants, and costs can be tested. This overview establishes the nouns, lifecycle, and invariants that later examples must make concrete. It is not yet the complete editorial treatment for every subtopic in this technology.
keyPoints: Name the execution unit and its lifecycle.
Identify the state and invariant owned by each abstraction.
Separate specification guarantees from common implementation behavior.

theorySections.title: Data, memory, and lifetime
theorySections.explanation: Computer Architecture programs move data through values, references, resources, or persisted representations. A strong explanation follows ownership and lifetime from creation through sharing, mutation, cleanup, and failure instead of relying on syntax alone.
keyPoints: Trace allocation and cleanup.
Make aliasing and mutation explicit.
Treat resource lifetime separately from garbage-collected memory where applicable.

theorySections.title: Concurrency and I/O
theorySections.explanation: Concurrency in Computer Architecture must be derived from its runtime and host platform. Explain what can execute independently, how work waits, how cancellation and backpressure propagate, and which synchronization rule protects shared invariants.
keyPoints: Distinguish concurrency from parallelism.
State the ordering or synchronization guarantee.
Bound queues, retries, and resource use.

theorySections.title: Production behavior
theorySections.explanation: A production Computer Architecture system is evaluated through tests, diagnostics, performance evidence, security boundaries, compatible changes, and recovery. Convenient abstractions are useful only when their hidden cost and failure signals remain observable.
keyPoints: Measure before optimizing.
Validate untrusted boundaries and use least privilege.
Design rollback, migration, and failure diagnosis with the feature.

misconceptions.claim: Computer Architecture best practices are universal rules.
misconceptions.correction: Practices are responses to constraints; state the workload, invariant, and trade-off before applying one.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Interview summaries often omit the forces that justify a recommendation.

misconceptions.claim: A successful Computer Architecture build proves runtime correctness.
misconceptions.correction: Build-time checks cover only declared contracts; runtime inputs, integration, resource limits, and concurrency still need evidence.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Fast local feedback is confused with end-to-end behavior.

misconceptions.claim: The most concise Computer Architecture API is automatically the most efficient.
misconceptions.correction: Abstractions can hide allocation, I/O, network calls, queries, synchronization, or retries; inspect and measure the execution path.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Source-code size is used as a proxy for work performed.

misconceptions.claim: Adding parallelism always speeds up Computer Architecture workloads.
misconceptions.correction: Useful parallelism is bounded by dependencies and resources; coordination, contention, queueing, and downstream limits can reduce throughput.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Available threads or workers are mistaken for additional system capacity.

revisionChecklist: Explain the Computer Architecture mental model without product slogans.
Name core types, lifecycle, invariants, and boundary conditions.
Trace one request or program from input through execution to output and cleanup.
State memory ownership, mutation, and resource-lifetime rules.
Explain concurrency, ordering, cancellation, and backpressure behavior.
Choose a test boundary and demonstrate an unhappy-path case.
Use one diagnostic tool and interpret its evidence.
Name a performance bottleneck, security risk, upgrade risk, and rollback path.
setup: Install from the official distribution or package manager.
Pin runtime and dependency versions in project metadata.
Run version, build, and test checks before changing code.
runtime: Name the execution unit and its lifecycle.
Trace allocation, scheduling, I/O, and cleanup.
Separate language or framework guarantees from implementation behavior.
testing: Test one behavior at the smallest stable boundary.
Keep deterministic unit tests separate from integration and end-to-end checks.
debugging: Reproduce with the smallest input and capture the first bad state.
Use structured logs, breakpoints, traces, or query plans before guessing.
performance: Measure latency, throughput, allocation, and contention before optimizing.
State the trade-off introduced by every cache, batch, pool, or parallel path.
security: Validate untrusted input at the boundary and use least privilege.
Keep secrets out of source, logs, command history, and generated artifacts.
failureModes: Using an unsupported or mismatched version.
Hiding an expensive operation behind a convenient abstraction.
Handling only the happy path while losing context from failures.

workedExamples.code: // Computer Architecture: smallest useful example
workedExamples.explanation: Trace inputs, state, and outputs before adding Computer Architecture abstractions.

workedExamples.title: Boundary made explicit
workedExamples.code:
// Computer Architecture: smallest useful example
// validate input and surface a useful failure
workedExamples.explanation: Move validation to the boundary so failures remain local and observable.

workedExamples.title: Testable production shape
workedExamples.code:
// Computer Architecture: smallest useful example
// inject dependencies; measure the result; cover the unhappy path
workedExamples.explanation: Separate policy from side effects, then test the contract rather than the implementation detail.

questions.prompt: Computer Architecture: Explain the runtime model without using framework slogans.
questions.answer: Start from the execution unit, state lifecycle, inputs, state, scheduling, outputs, and cleanup; then separate specified guarantees from one implementation.
questions.whyTricky: Fluent API usage can hide a weak execution model.
rubric: Defines the relevant mechanism and invariant.
Uses a concrete example and names a trade-off.

theorySections.title: Data, memory, and lifetime
theorySections.explanation: Compilers programs move data through values, references, resources, or persisted representations. A strong explanation follows ownership and lifetime from creation through sharing, mutation, cleanup, and failure instead of relying on syntax alone.

theorySections.title: Concurrency and I/O

theorySections.title: Production behavior

theorySections.title: Core abstraction
theorySections.explanation: React is best understood as a set of boundaries, lifecycle rules, and failure modes—not a list of APIs. Trace one request or unit of work through those boundaries. This overview establishes the nouns, lifecycle, and invariants that later examples must make concrete. It is not yet the complete editorial treatment for every subtopic in this technology.
keyPoints: Name the execution unit and its lifecycle.
Identify the state and invariant owned by each abstraction.
Separate specification guarantees from common implementation behavior.

theorySections.title: Data, memory, and lifetime
theorySections.explanation: React programs move data through values, references, resources, or persisted representations. A strong explanation follows ownership and lifetime from creation through sharing, mutation, cleanup, and failure instead of relying on syntax alone.
keyPoints: Trace allocation and cleanup.
Make aliasing and mutation explicit.
Treat resource lifetime separately from garbage-collected memory where applicable.

theorySections.title: Concurrency and I/O
theorySections.explanation: Concurrency in React must be derived from its runtime and host platform. Explain what can execute independently, how work waits, how cancellation and backpressure propagate, and which synchronization rule protects shared invariants.
keyPoints: Distinguish concurrency from parallelism.
State the ordering or synchronization guarantee.
Bound queues, retries, and resource use.

theorySections.title: Production behavior
theorySections.explanation: A production React system is evaluated through tests, diagnostics, performance evidence, security boundaries, compatible changes, and recovery. Convenient abstractions are useful only when their hidden cost and failure signals remain observable.
keyPoints: Measure before optimizing.
Validate untrusted boundaries and use least privilege.
Design rollback, migration, and failure diagnosis with the feature.

misconceptions.claim: React best practices are universal rules.
misconceptions.correction: Practices are responses to constraints; state the workload, invariant, and trade-off before applying one.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Interview summaries often omit the forces that justify a recommendation.

misconceptions.claim: A successful React build proves runtime correctness.
misconceptions.correction: Build-time checks cover only declared contracts; runtime inputs, integration, resource limits, and concurrency still need evidence.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Fast local feedback is confused with end-to-end behavior.

misconceptions.claim: The most concise React API is automatically the most efficient.
misconceptions.correction: Abstractions can hide allocation, I/O, network calls, queries, synchronization, or retries; inspect and measure the execution path.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Source-code size is used as a proxy for work performed.

misconceptions.claim: Adding parallelism always speeds up React workloads.
misconceptions.correction: Useful parallelism is bounded by dependencies and resources; coordination, contention, queueing, and downstream limits can reduce throughput.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Available threads or workers are mistaken for additional system capacity.

theorySections.title: Core abstraction
theorySections.explanation: Vue is best understood as a set of boundaries, lifecycle rules, and failure modes—not a list of APIs. Trace one request or unit of work through those boundaries. This overview establishes the nouns, lifecycle, and invariants that later examples must make concrete. It is not yet the complete editorial treatment for every subtopic in this technology.
keyPoints: Name the execution unit and its lifecycle.
Identify the state and invariant owned by each abstraction.
Separate specification guarantees from common implementation behavior.

theorySections.title: Data, memory, and lifetime
theorySections.explanation: Vue programs move data through values, references, resources, or persisted representations. A strong explanation follows ownership and lifetime from creation through sharing, mutation, cleanup, and failure instead of relying on syntax alone.
keyPoints: Trace allocation and cleanup.
Make aliasing and mutation explicit.
Treat resource lifetime separately from garbage-collected memory where applicable.

theorySections.title: Concurrency and I/O
theorySections.explanation: Concurrency in Vue must be derived from its runtime and host platform. Explain what can execute independently, how work waits, how cancellation and backpressure propagate, and which synchronization rule protects shared invariants.
keyPoints: Distinguish concurrency from parallelism.
State the ordering or synchronization guarantee.
Bound queues, retries, and resource use.

theorySections.title: Production behavior
theorySections.explanation: A production Vue system is evaluated through tests, diagnostics, performance evidence, security boundaries, compatible changes, and recovery. Convenient abstractions are useful only when their hidden cost and failure signals remain observable.
keyPoints: Measure before optimizing.
Validate untrusted boundaries and use least privilege.
Design rollback, migration, and failure diagnosis with the feature.

misconceptions.claim: Vue best practices are universal rules.
misconceptions.correction: Practices are responses to constraints; state the workload, invariant, and trade-off before applying one.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Interview summaries often omit the forces that justify a recommendation.

misconceptions.claim: A successful Vue build proves runtime correctness.
misconceptions.correction: Build-time checks cover only declared contracts; runtime inputs, integration, resource limits, and concurrency still need evidence.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Fast local feedback is confused with end-to-end behavior.

misconceptions.claim: The most concise Vue API is automatically the most efficient.
misconceptions.correction: Abstractions can hide allocation, I/O, network calls, queries, synchronization, or retries; inspect and measure the execution path.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Source-code size is used as a proxy for work performed.

misconceptions.claim: Adding parallelism always speeds up Vue workloads.
misconceptions.correction: Useful parallelism is bounded by dependencies and resources; coordination, contention, queueing, and downstream limits can reduce throughput.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Available threads or workers are mistaken for additional system capacity.

theorySections.title: Core abstraction
theorySections.explanation: SvelteKit is best understood as a set of boundaries, lifecycle rules, and failure modes—not a list of APIs. Trace one request or unit of work through those boundaries. This overview establishes the nouns, lifecycle, and invariants that later examples must make concrete. It is not yet the complete editorial treatment for every subtopic in this technology.
keyPoints: Name the execution unit and its lifecycle.
Identify the state and invariant owned by each abstraction.
Separate specification guarantees from common implementation behavior.

theorySections.title: Data, memory, and lifetime
theorySections.explanation: SvelteKit programs move data through values, references, resources, or persisted representations. A strong explanation follows ownership and lifetime from creation through sharing, mutation, cleanup, and failure instead of relying on syntax alone.
keyPoints: Trace allocation and cleanup.
Make aliasing and mutation explicit.
Treat resource lifetime separately from garbage-collected memory where applicable.

theorySections.title: Concurrency and I/O
theorySections.explanation: Concurrency in SvelteKit must be derived from its runtime and host platform. Explain what can execute independently, how work waits, how cancellation and backpressure propagate, and which synchronization rule protects shared invariants.
keyPoints: Distinguish concurrency from parallelism.
State the ordering or synchronization guarantee.
Bound queues, retries, and resource use.

theorySections.title: Production behavior
theorySections.explanation: A production SvelteKit system is evaluated through tests, diagnostics, performance evidence, security boundaries, compatible changes, and recovery. Convenient abstractions are useful only when their hidden cost and failure signals remain observable.
keyPoints: Measure before optimizing.
Validate untrusted boundaries and use least privilege.
Design rollback, migration, and failure diagnosis with the feature.

misconceptions.claim: SvelteKit best practices are universal rules.
misconceptions.correction: Practices are responses to constraints; state the workload, invariant, and trade-off before applying one.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Interview summaries often omit the forces that justify a recommendation.

misconceptions.claim: A successful SvelteKit build proves runtime correctness.
misconceptions.correction: Build-time checks cover only declared contracts; runtime inputs, integration, resource limits, and concurrency still need evidence.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Fast local feedback is confused with end-to-end behavior.

misconceptions.claim: The most concise SvelteKit API is automatically the most efficient.
misconceptions.correction: Abstractions can hide allocation, I/O, network calls, queries, synchronization, or retries; inspect and measure the execution path.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Source-code size is used as a proxy for work performed.

misconceptions.claim: Adding parallelism always speeds up SvelteKit workloads.
misconceptions.correction: Useful parallelism is bounded by dependencies and resources; coordination, contention, queueing, and downstream limits can reduce throughput.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Available threads or workers are mistaken for additional system capacity.

theorySections.title: Core abstraction
theorySections.explanation: NestJS is best understood as a set of boundaries, lifecycle rules, and failure modes—not a list of APIs. Trace one request or unit of work through those boundaries. This overview establishes the nouns, lifecycle, and invariants that later examples must make concrete. It is not yet the complete editorial treatment for every subtopic in this technology.
keyPoints: Name the execution unit and its lifecycle.
Identify the state and invariant owned by each abstraction.
Separate specification guarantees from common implementation behavior.

theorySections.title: Data, memory, and lifetime
theorySections.explanation: NestJS programs move data through values, references, resources, or persisted representations. A strong explanation follows ownership and lifetime from creation through sharing, mutation, cleanup, and failure instead of relying on syntax alone.
keyPoints: Trace allocation and cleanup.
Make aliasing and mutation explicit.
Treat resource lifetime separately from garbage-collected memory where applicable.

theorySections.title: Concurrency and I/O
theorySections.explanation: Concurrency in NestJS must be derived from its runtime and host platform. Explain what can execute independently, how work waits, how cancellation and backpressure propagate, and which synchronization rule protects shared invariants.
keyPoints: Distinguish concurrency from parallelism.
State the ordering or synchronization guarantee.
Bound queues, retries, and resource use.

theorySections.title: Production behavior
theorySections.explanation: A production NestJS system is evaluated through tests, diagnostics, performance evidence, security boundaries, compatible changes, and recovery. Convenient abstractions are useful only when their hidden cost and failure signals remain observable.
keyPoints: Measure before optimizing.
Validate untrusted boundaries and use least privilege.
Design rollback, migration, and failure diagnosis with the feature.

misconceptions.claim: NestJS best practices are universal rules.
misconceptions.correction: Practices are responses to constraints; state the workload, invariant, and trade-off before applying one.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Interview summaries often omit the forces that justify a recommendation.

misconceptions.claim: A successful NestJS build proves runtime correctness.
misconceptions.correction: Build-time checks cover only declared contracts; runtime inputs, integration, resource limits, and concurrency still need evidence.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Fast local feedback is confused with end-to-end behavior.

misconceptions.claim: The most concise NestJS API is automatically the most efficient.
misconceptions.correction: Abstractions can hide allocation, I/O, network calls, queries, synchronization, or retries; inspect and measure the execution path.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Source-code size is used as a proxy for work performed.

misconceptions.claim: Adding parallelism always speeds up NestJS workloads.
misconceptions.correction: Useful parallelism is bounded by dependencies and resources; coordination, contention, queueing, and downstream limits can reduce throughput.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Available threads or workers are mistaken for additional system capacity.

Trace one request or program from input through execution to output and cleanup.
State memory ownership, mutation, and resource-lifetime rules.
Explain concurrency, ordering, cancellation, and backpressure behavior.
Choose a test boundary and demonstrate an unhappy-path case.
Use one diagnostic tool and interpret its evidence.

runtime: Name the execution unit and its lifecycle.
Trace allocation, scheduling, I/O, and cleanup.
Separate language or framework guarantees from implementation behavior.
testing: Test one behavior at the smallest stable boundary.
Keep deterministic unit tests separate from integration and end-to-end checks.
debugging: Reproduce with the smallest input and capture the first bad state.
Use structured logs, breakpoints, traces, or query plans before guessing.
performance: Measure latency, throughput, allocation, and contention before optimizing.
State the trade-off introduced by every cache, batch, pool, or parallel path.
security: Validate untrusted input at the boundary and use least privilege.
Keep secrets out of source, logs, command history, and generated artifacts.
failureModes: Using an unsupported or mismatched version.

Handling only the happy path while losing context from failures.

questions.prompt: NestJS: What is the safest upgrade path between supported versions?

Includes a failure signal or verification method.

questions.answer: Define identities, least privilege, secret delivery, trusted artifacts, input boundaries, audit signals, staged rollout, compatibility window, rollback trigger, and recovery verification.

misconceptions.claim: A successful Flask build proves runtime correctness.

misconceptions.whyItHappens: Fast local feedback is confused with end-to-end behavior.

misconceptions.claim: The most concise Flask API is automatically the most efficient.

theorySections.title: Data, memory, and lifetime
theorySections.explanation: FastAPI programs move data through values, references, resources, or persisted representations. A strong explanation follows ownership and lifetime from creation through sharing, mutation, cleanup, and failure instead of relying on syntax alone.
keyPoints: Trace allocation and cleanup.
Make aliasing and mutation explicit.
Treat resource lifetime separately from garbage-collected memory where applicable.

theorySections.title: Concurrency and I/O
theorySections.explanation: Concurrency in FastAPI must be derived from its runtime and host platform. Explain what can execute independently, how work waits, how cancellation and backpressure propagate, and which synchronization rule protects shared invariants.

State the ordering or synchronization guarantee.
Bound queues, retries, and resource use.

theorySections.title: Production behavior
theorySections.explanation: A production FastAPI system is evaluated through tests, diagnostics, performance evidence, security boundaries, compatible changes, and recovery. Convenient abstractions are useful only when their hidden cost and failure signals remain observable.
keyPoints: Measure before optimizing.
Validate untrusted boundaries and use least privilege.
Design rollback, migration, and failure diagnosis with the feature.

theorySections.title: Core abstraction
theorySections.explanation: Go net/http is best understood as a set of boundaries, lifecycle rules, and failure modes—not a list of APIs. Trace one request or unit of work through those boundaries. This overview establishes the nouns, lifecycle, and invariants that later examples must make concrete. It is not yet the complete editorial treatment for every subtopic in this technology.
keyPoints: Name the execution unit and its lifecycle.
Identify the state and invariant owned by each abstraction.
Separate specification guarantees from common implementation behavior.

theorySections.title: Data, memory, and lifetime
theorySections.explanation: Go net/http programs move data through values, references, resources, or persisted representations. A strong explanation follows ownership and lifetime from creation through sharing, mutation, cleanup, and failure instead of relying on syntax alone.
keyPoints: Trace allocation and cleanup.
Make aliasing and mutation explicit.
Treat resource lifetime separately from garbage-collected memory where applicable.

theorySections.title: Concurrency and I/O
theorySections.explanation: Concurrency in Go net/http must be derived from its runtime and host platform. Explain what can execute independently, how work waits, how cancellation and backpressure propagate, and which synchronization rule protects shared invariants.
keyPoints: Distinguish concurrency from parallelism.
State the ordering or synchronization guarantee.
Bound queues, retries, and resource use.

theorySections.title: Production behavior
theorySections.explanation: A production Go net/http system is evaluated through tests, diagnostics, performance evidence, security boundaries, compatible changes, and recovery. Convenient abstractions are useful only when their hidden cost and failure signals remain observable.
keyPoints: Measure before optimizing.
Validate untrusted boundaries and use least privilege.
Design rollback, migration, and failure diagnosis with the feature.

misconceptions.claim: Go net/http best practices are universal rules.
misconceptions.correction: Practices are responses to constraints; state the workload, invariant, and trade-off before applying one.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Interview summaries often omit the forces that justify a recommendation.

misconceptions.claim: A successful Go net/http build proves runtime correctness.
misconceptions.correction: Build-time checks cover only declared contracts; runtime inputs, integration, resource limits, and concurrency still need evidence.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Fast local feedback is confused with end-to-end behavior.

misconceptions.claim: The most concise Go net/http API is automatically the most efficient.
misconceptions.correction: Abstractions can hide allocation, I/O, network calls, queries, synchronization, or retries; inspect and measure the execution path.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Source-code size is used as a proxy for work performed.

misconceptions.claim: Adding parallelism always speeds up Go net/http workloads.
misconceptions.correction: Useful parallelism is bounded by dependencies and resources; coordination, contention, queueing, and downstream limits can reduce throughput.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Available threads or workers are mistaken for additional system capacity.

theorySections.title: Core abstraction
theorySections.explanation: Axum is best understood as a set of boundaries, lifecycle rules, and failure modes—not a list of APIs. Trace one request or unit of work through those boundaries. This overview establishes the nouns, lifecycle, and invariants that later examples must make concrete. It is not yet the complete editorial treatment for every subtopic in this technology.
keyPoints: Name the execution unit and its lifecycle.
Identify the state and invariant owned by each abstraction.
Separate specification guarantees from common implementation behavior.

theorySections.title: Data, memory, and lifetime
theorySections.explanation: Axum programs move data through values, references, resources, or persisted representations. A strong explanation follows ownership and lifetime from creation through sharing, mutation, cleanup, and failure instead of relying on syntax alone.
keyPoints: Trace allocation and cleanup.
Make aliasing and mutation explicit.
Treat resource lifetime separately from garbage-collected memory where applicable.

theorySections.title: Concurrency and I/O
theorySections.explanation: Concurrency in Axum must be derived from its runtime and host platform. Explain what can execute independently, how work waits, how cancellation and backpressure propagate, and which synchronization rule protects shared invariants.
keyPoints: Distinguish concurrency from parallelism.
State the ordering or synchronization guarantee.
Bound queues, retries, and resource use.

theorySections.title: Production behavior
theorySections.explanation: A production Axum system is evaluated through tests, diagnostics, performance evidence, security boundaries, compatible changes, and recovery. Convenient abstractions are useful only when their hidden cost and failure signals remain observable.
keyPoints: Measure before optimizing.
Validate untrusted boundaries and use least privilege.
Design rollback, migration, and failure diagnosis with the feature.

misconceptions.claim: Axum best practices are universal rules.
misconceptions.correction: Practices are responses to constraints; state the workload, invariant, and trade-off before applying one.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Interview summaries often omit the forces that justify a recommendation.

misconceptions.claim: A successful Axum build proves runtime correctness.
misconceptions.correction: Build-time checks cover only declared contracts; runtime inputs, integration, resource limits, and concurrency still need evidence.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Fast local feedback is confused with end-to-end behavior.

misconceptions.claim: The most concise Axum API is automatically the most efficient.
misconceptions.correction: Abstractions can hide allocation, I/O, network calls, queries, synchronization, or retries; inspect and measure the execution path.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Source-code size is used as a proxy for work performed.

misconceptions.claim: Adding parallelism always speeds up Axum workloads.
misconceptions.correction: Useful parallelism is bounded by dependencies and resources; coordination, contention, queueing, and downstream limits can reduce throughput.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Available threads or workers are mistaken for additional system capacity.

theorySections.title: Core abstraction
theorySections.explanation: Ruby on Rails is best understood as a set of boundaries, lifecycle rules, and failure modes—not a list of APIs. Trace one request or unit of work through those boundaries. This overview establishes the nouns, lifecycle, and invariants that later examples must make concrete. It is not yet the complete editorial treatment for every subtopic in this technology.
keyPoints: Name the execution unit and its lifecycle.
Identify the state and invariant owned by each abstraction.
Separate specification guarantees from common implementation behavior.

theorySections.title: Data, memory, and lifetime
theorySections.explanation: Ruby on Rails programs move data through values, references, resources, or persisted representations. A strong explanation follows ownership and lifetime from creation through sharing, mutation, cleanup, and failure instead of relying on syntax alone.
keyPoints: Trace allocation and cleanup.
Make aliasing and mutation explicit.
Treat resource lifetime separately from garbage-collected memory where applicable.

theorySections.title: Concurrency and I/O
theorySections.explanation: Concurrency in Ruby on Rails must be derived from its runtime and host platform. Explain what can execute independently, how work waits, how cancellation and backpressure propagate, and which synchronization rule protects shared invariants.
keyPoints: Distinguish concurrency from parallelism.
State the ordering or synchronization guarantee.
Bound queues, retries, and resource use.

theorySections.title: Production behavior
theorySections.explanation: A production Ruby on Rails system is evaluated through tests, diagnostics, performance evidence, security boundaries, compatible changes, and recovery. Convenient abstractions are useful only when their hidden cost and failure signals remain observable.
keyPoints: Measure before optimizing.
Validate untrusted boundaries and use least privilege.
Design rollback, migration, and failure diagnosis with the feature.

misconceptions.claim: Ruby on Rails best practices are universal rules.
misconceptions.correction: Practices are responses to constraints; state the workload, invariant, and trade-off before applying one.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Interview summaries often omit the forces that justify a recommendation.

misconceptions.claim: A successful Ruby on Rails build proves runtime correctness.
misconceptions.correction: Build-time checks cover only declared contracts; runtime inputs, integration, resource limits, and concurrency still need evidence.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Fast local feedback is confused with end-to-end behavior.

misconceptions.claim: The most concise Ruby on Rails API is automatically the most efficient.
misconceptions.correction: Abstractions can hide allocation, I/O, network calls, queries, synchronization, or retries; inspect and measure the execution path.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Source-code size is used as a proxy for work performed.

misconceptions.claim: Adding parallelism always speeds up Ruby on Rails workloads.
misconceptions.correction: Useful parallelism is bounded by dependencies and resources; coordination, contention, queueing, and downstream limits can reduce throughput.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Available threads or workers are mistaken for additional system capacity.

theorySections.title: Core abstraction
theorySections.explanation: PostgreSQL is best understood as a set of boundaries, lifecycle rules, and failure modes—not a list of APIs. Trace one request or unit of work through those boundaries. This overview establishes the nouns, lifecycle, and invariants that later examples must make concrete. It is not yet the complete editorial treatment for every subtopic in this technology.
keyPoints: Name the execution unit and its lifecycle.
Identify the state and invariant owned by each abstraction.
Separate specification guarantees from common implementation behavior.

theorySections.title: Data, memory, and lifetime
theorySections.explanation: PostgreSQL programs move data through values, references, resources, or persisted representations. A strong explanation follows ownership and lifetime from creation through sharing, mutation, cleanup, and failure instead of relying on syntax alone.
keyPoints: Trace allocation and cleanup.
Make aliasing and mutation explicit.
Treat resource lifetime separately from garbage-collected memory where applicable.

theorySections.title: Concurrency and I/O
theorySections.explanation: Concurrency in PostgreSQL must be derived from its runtime and host platform. Explain what can execute independently, how work waits, how cancellation and backpressure propagate, and which synchronization rule protects shared invariants.
keyPoints: Distinguish concurrency from parallelism.
State the ordering or synchronization guarantee.
Bound queues, retries, and resource use.

theorySections.title: Production behavior
theorySections.explanation: A production PostgreSQL system is evaluated through tests, diagnostics, performance evidence, security boundaries, compatible changes, and recovery. Convenient abstractions are useful only when their hidden cost and failure signals remain observable.
keyPoints: Measure before optimizing.
Validate untrusted boundaries and use least privilege.
Design rollback, migration, and failure diagnosis with the feature.

misconceptions.claim: PostgreSQL best practices are universal rules.
misconceptions.correction: Practices are responses to constraints; state the workload, invariant, and trade-off before applying one.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Interview summaries often omit the forces that justify a recommendation.

misconceptions.claim: A successful PostgreSQL build proves runtime correctness.
misconceptions.correction: Build-time checks cover only declared contracts; runtime inputs, integration, resource limits, and concurrency still need evidence.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Fast local feedback is confused with end-to-end behavior.

misconceptions.claim: The most concise PostgreSQL API is automatically the most efficient.
misconceptions.correction: Abstractions can hide allocation, I/O, network calls, queries, synchronization, or retries; inspect and measure the execution path.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Source-code size is used as a proxy for work performed.

misconceptions.claim: Adding parallelism always speeds up PostgreSQL workloads.
misconceptions.correction: Useful parallelism is bounded by dependencies and resources; coordination, contention, queueing, and downstream limits can reduce throughput.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Available threads or workers are mistaken for additional system capacity.

theorySections.title: Core abstraction
theorySections.explanation: Neo4j is best understood as a set of boundaries, lifecycle rules, and failure modes—not a list of APIs. Trace one request or unit of work through those boundaries. This overview establishes the nouns, lifecycle, and invariants that later examples must make concrete. It is not yet the complete editorial treatment for every subtopic in this technology.
keyPoints: Name the execution unit and its lifecycle.
Identify the state and invariant owned by each abstraction.
Separate specification guarantees from common implementation behavior.

theorySections.title: Data, memory, and lifetime
theorySections.explanation: Neo4j programs move data through values, references, resources, or persisted representations. A strong explanation follows ownership and lifetime from creation through sharing, mutation, cleanup, and failure instead of relying on syntax alone.
keyPoints: Trace allocation and cleanup.
Make aliasing and mutation explicit.
Treat resource lifetime separately from garbage-collected memory where applicable.

theorySections.title: Concurrency and I/O
theorySections.explanation: Concurrency in Neo4j must be derived from its runtime and host platform. Explain what can execute independently, how work waits, how cancellation and backpressure propagate, and which synchronization rule protects shared invariants.
keyPoints: Distinguish concurrency from parallelism.
State the ordering or synchronization guarantee.
Bound queues, retries, and resource use.

theorySections.title: Production behavior
theorySections.explanation: A production Neo4j system is evaluated through tests, diagnostics, performance evidence, security boundaries, compatible changes, and recovery. Convenient abstractions are useful only when their hidden cost and failure signals remain observable.
keyPoints: Measure before optimizing.
Validate untrusted boundaries and use least privilege.
Design rollback, migration, and failure diagnosis with the feature.

misconceptions.claim: Neo4j best practices are universal rules.
misconceptions.correction: Practices are responses to constraints; state the workload, invariant, and trade-off before applying one.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Interview summaries often omit the forces that justify a recommendation.

misconceptions.claim: A successful Neo4j build proves runtime correctness.
misconceptions.correction: Build-time checks cover only declared contracts; runtime inputs, integration, resource limits, and concurrency still need evidence.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Fast local feedback is confused with end-to-end behavior.

misconceptions.claim: The most concise Neo4j API is automatically the most efficient.
misconceptions.correction: Abstractions can hide allocation, I/O, network calls, queries, synchronization, or retries; inspect and measure the execution path.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Source-code size is used as a proxy for work performed.

misconceptions.claim: Adding parallelism always speeds up Neo4j workloads.
misconceptions.correction: Useful parallelism is bounded by dependencies and resources; coordination, contention, queueing, and downstream limits can reduce throughput.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Available threads or workers are mistaken for additional system capacity.

version.policy: Use a supported stable release; verify the project lockfile before an interview exercise.

technologies.mentalModel: Selenium is best understood as a set of boundaries, lifecycle rules, and failure modes—not a list of APIs. Trace one request or unit of work through those boundaries.

learningPath.title: Foundations
learningPath.objective: Build a correct vocabulary and smallest working Selenium program.

learningPath.title: Working fluency
learningPath.objective: Use Selenium idiomatically in tested application code.

theorySections.title: Core abstraction
theorySections.explanation: Selenium is best understood as a set of boundaries, lifecycle rules, and failure modes—not a list of APIs. Trace one request or unit of work through those boundaries. This overview establishes the nouns, lifecycle, and invariants that later examples must make concrete. It is not yet the complete editorial treatment for every subtopic in this technology.
keyPoints: Name the execution unit and its lifecycle.
Identify the state and invariant owned by each abstraction.
Separate specification guarantees from common implementation behavior.

theorySections.title: Data, memory, and lifetime
theorySections.explanation: Selenium programs move data through values, references, resources, or persisted representations. A strong explanation follows ownership and lifetime from creation through sharing, mutation, cleanup, and failure instead of relying on syntax alone.
keyPoints: Trace allocation and cleanup.
Make aliasing and mutation explicit.
Treat resource lifetime separately from garbage-collected memory where applicable.

theorySections.title: Concurrency and I/O
theorySections.explanation: Concurrency in Selenium must be derived from its runtime and host platform. Explain what can execute independently, how work waits, how cancellation and backpressure propagate, and which synchronization rule protects shared invariants.
keyPoints: Distinguish concurrency from parallelism.
State the ordering or synchronization guarantee.
Bound queues, retries, and resource use.

theorySections.title: Production behavior
theorySections.explanation: A production Selenium system is evaluated through tests, diagnostics, performance evidence, security boundaries, compatible changes, and recovery. Convenient abstractions are useful only when their hidden cost and failure signals remain observable.
keyPoints: Measure before optimizing.
Validate untrusted boundaries and use least privilege.
Design rollback, migration, and failure diagnosis with the feature.

misconceptions.claim: Selenium best practices are universal rules.
misconceptions.correction: Practices are responses to constraints; state the workload, invariant, and trade-off before applying one.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Interview summaries often omit the forces that justify a recommendation.

misconceptions.claim: A successful Selenium build proves runtime correctness.
misconceptions.correction: Build-time checks cover only declared contracts; runtime inputs, integration, resource limits, and concurrency still need evidence.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Fast local feedback is confused with end-to-end behavior.

misconceptions.claim: The most concise Selenium API is automatically the most efficient.
misconceptions.correction: Abstractions can hide allocation, I/O, network calls, queries, synchronization, or retries; inspect and measure the execution path.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Source-code size is used as a proxy for work performed.

misconceptions.claim: Adding parallelism always speeds up Selenium workloads.
misconceptions.correction: Useful parallelism is bounded by dependencies and resources; coordination, contention, queueing, and downstream limits can reduce throughput.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Available threads or workers are mistaken for additional system capacity.

revisionChecklist: Explain the Selenium mental model without product slogans.
Name core types, lifecycle, invariants, and boundary conditions.
Trace one request or program from input through execution to output and cleanup.
State memory ownership, mutation, and resource-lifetime rules.
Explain concurrency, ordering, cancellation, and backpressure behavior.
Choose a test boundary and demonstrate an unhappy-path case.
Use one diagnostic tool and interpret its evidence.
Name a performance bottleneck, security risk, upgrade risk, and rollback path.
setup: Install from the official distribution or package manager.
Pin runtime and dependency versions in project metadata.
Run version, build, and test checks before changing code.
runtime: Name the execution unit and its lifecycle.
Trace allocation, scheduling, I/O, and cleanup.
Separate language or framework guarantees from implementation behavior.
testing: Test one behavior at the smallest stable boundary.
Keep deterministic unit tests separate from integration and end-to-end checks.
debugging: Reproduce with the smallest input and capture the first bad state.
Use structured logs, breakpoints, traces, or query plans before guessing.
performance: Measure latency, throughput, allocation, and contention before optimizing.
State the trade-off introduced by every cache, batch, pool, or parallel path.
security: Validate untrusted input at the boundary and use least privilege.
Keep secrets out of source, logs, command history, and generated artifacts.
failureModes: Using an unsupported or mismatched version.
Hiding an expensive operation behind a convenient abstraction.
Handling only the happy path while losing context from failures.

workedExamples.code: // Selenium: isolate the framework boundary behind a small application-facing interface.
workedExamples.explanation: A thin boundary keeps domain behavior testable and makes lifecycle and failure behavior visible.

workedExamples.code:

workedExamples.explanation: Move validation to the boundary so failures remain local and observable.

workedExamples.title: Testable production shape
workedExamples.code:
// Selenium: isolate the framework boundary behind a small application-facing interface.
// inject dependencies; measure the result; cover the unhappy path
workedExamples.explanation: Separate policy from side effects, then test the contract rather than the implementation detail.

questions.prompt: Selenium: Explain the runtime model without using framework slogans.
questions.answer: Start from the execution unit, state lifecycle, inputs, state, scheduling, outputs, and cleanup; then separate specified guarantees from one implementation.
questions.whyTricky: Fluent API usage can hide a weak execution model.
rubric: Defines the relevant mechanism and invariant.
Uses a concrete example and names a trade-off.
Includes a failure signal or verification method.

questions.prompt: Selenium: Which guarantees belong to the specification and which to the implementation?
questions.answer: Name each relied-on behavior, cite whether it is contractual, and explain how version or implementation changes would affect it.
questions.whyTricky: Familiar behavior is often mistaken for a portable guarantee.
rubric: Defines the relevant mechanism and invariant.
Uses a concrete example and names a trade-off.
Includes a failure signal or verification method.

questions.prompt: Selenium: Design a minimal test pyramid for a production feature.
questions.answer: Use deterministic unit tests for policy, integration tests for real boundaries, a few end-to-end journeys, and contract or property tests where interfaces or invariants need them.
questions.whyTricky: Test labels are less important than stable boundaries and failure coverage.
rubric: Defines the relevant mechanism and invariant.
Uses a concrete example and names a trade-off.
Includes a failure signal or verification method.

questions.prompt: Selenium: Diagnose a latency regression using evidence rather than guesses.
questions.answer: Reproduce under comparable load, decompose the latency budget, inspect traces and resource saturation, profile the constrained stage, change one cause, and verify tail as well as median latency.
questions.whyTricky: Average timing and correlation frequently produce false diagnoses.
rubric: Defines the relevant mechanism and invariant.
Uses a concrete example and names a trade-off.
Includes a failure signal or verification method.

questions.prompt: Selenium: Name three failure modes and the signal that reveals each one.
questions.answer: Choose distinct correctness, resource, and integration failures and pair each with an observable log, metric, trace, state inspection, or failed invariant.
questions.whyTricky: Generic failure lists without discriminating evidence are not actionable.
rubric: Defines the relevant mechanism and invariant.
Uses a concrete example and names a trade-off.
Includes a failure signal or verification method.

questions.prompt: Selenium: How do memory, concurrency, and I/O interact here?
questions.answer: Trace allocation and ownership across scheduled work and blocking or asynchronous boundaries, including queues, buffering, cancellation, cleanup, and backpressure.
questions.whyTricky: These resources are usually taught separately even though production failures couple them.
rubric: Defines the relevant mechanism and invariant.
Uses a concrete example and names a trade-off.
Includes a failure signal or verification method.

questions.prompt: Selenium: What is the safest upgrade path between supported versions?
questions.answer: Read compatibility notes, pin inputs, test representative behavior, stage the rollout, observe agreed signals, retain rollback, and migrate data or APIs in compatible phases.
questions.whyTricky: A green build does not prove behavioral or operational compatibility.
rubric: Defines the relevant mechanism and invariant.
Uses a concrete example and names a trade-off.
Includes a failure signal or verification method.

questions.prompt: Selenium: Sketch a secure deployment and rollback strategy.
questions.answer: Define identities, least privilege, secret delivery, trusted artifacts, input boundaries, audit signals, staged rollout, compatibility window, rollback trigger, and recovery verification.
questions.whyTricky: Deployment safety spans code, identity, data, and operational state.
rubric: Defines the relevant mechanism and invariant.
Uses a concrete example and names a trade-off.
Includes a failure signal or verification method.

flashcards.back: Selenium is best understood as a set of boundaries, lifecycle rules, and failure modes—not a list of APIs. Trace one request or unit of work through those boundaries.
Reproduce narrowly and inspect the first incorrect state.
Measure the constrained resource before changing the design.
Treat input and identity as untrusted until validated at a boundary.
Name the shared invariant, its owner, and the ordering mechanism.
Test behavior at the smallest stable boundary and include the unhappy path.
Pin, read compatibility notes, stage, observe, and keep a tested rollback.
Model → invariant → mechanism → example → trade-off → failure signal.

misconceptions.claim: Adding parallelism always speeds up Jetpack Compose workloads.

Separate specification guarantees from common implementation behavior.

theorySections.title: Data, memory, and lifetime
theorySections.explanation: iOS programs move data through values, references, resources, or persisted representations. A strong explanation follows ownership and lifetime from creation through sharing, mutation, cleanup, and failure instead of relying on syntax alone.
keyPoints: Trace allocation and cleanup.
Make aliasing and mutation explicit.
Treat resource lifetime separately from garbage-collected memory where applicable.

theorySections.title: Concurrency and I/O

State the ordering or synchronization guarantee.
Bound queues, retries, and resource use.

Design rollback, migration, and failure diagnosis with the feature.

theorySections.explanation: Flutter is an operational system with inputs, state, lifecycle, resource limits, and observable failure signals. Trace those five things before memorizing APIs. This overview establishes the nouns, lifecycle, and invariants that later examples must make concrete. It is not yet the complete editorial treatment for every subtopic in this technology.
keyPoints: Name the execution unit and its lifecycle.

Separate specification guarantees from common implementation behavior.

theorySections.title: Data, memory, and lifetime
theorySections.explanation: Flutter programs move data through values, references, resources, or persisted representations. A strong explanation follows ownership and lifetime from creation through sharing, mutation, cleanup, and failure instead of relying on syntax alone.
keyPoints: Trace allocation and cleanup.

theorySections.title: Concurrency and I/O
theorySections.explanation: Concurrency in Flutter must be derived from its runtime and host platform. Explain what can execute independently, how work waits, how cancellation and backpressure propagate, and which synchronization rule protects shared invariants.
keyPoints: Distinguish concurrency from parallelism.
State the ordering or synchronization guarantee.
Bound queues, retries, and resource use.

theorySections.title: Production behavior
theorySections.explanation: A production Flutter system is evaluated through tests, diagnostics, performance evidence, security boundaries, compatible changes, and recovery. Convenient abstractions are useful only when their hidden cost and failure signals remain observable.
keyPoints: Measure before optimizing.
Validate untrusted boundaries and use least privilege.
Design rollback, migration, and failure diagnosis with the feature.

misconceptions.claim: Flutter best practices are universal rules.
misconceptions.correction: Practices are responses to constraints; state the workload, invariant, and trade-off before applying one.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Interview summaries often omit the forces that justify a recommendation.

misconceptions.claim: A successful Flutter build proves runtime correctness.
misconceptions.correction: Build-time checks cover only declared contracts; runtime inputs, integration, resource limits, and concurrency still need evidence.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Fast local feedback is confused with end-to-end behavior.

misconceptions.claim: The most concise Flutter API is automatically the most efficient.
misconceptions.correction: Abstractions can hide allocation, I/O, network calls, queries, synchronization, or retries; inspect and measure the execution path.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Source-code size is used as a proxy for work performed.

misconceptions.claim: Adding parallelism always speeds up Flutter workloads.
misconceptions.correction: Useful parallelism is bounded by dependencies and resources; coordination, contention, queueing, and downstream limits can reduce throughput.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Available threads or workers are mistaken for additional system capacity.

theorySections.title: Core abstraction
theorySections.explanation: Hugging Face is an operational system with inputs, state, lifecycle, resource limits, and observable failure signals. Trace those five things before memorizing APIs. This overview establishes the nouns, lifecycle, and invariants that later examples must make concrete. It is not yet the complete editorial treatment for every subtopic in this technology.
keyPoints: Name the execution unit and its lifecycle.
Identify the state and invariant owned by each abstraction.
Separate specification guarantees from common implementation behavior.

theorySections.title: Data, memory, and lifetime
theorySections.explanation: Hugging Face programs move data through values, references, resources, or persisted representations. A strong explanation follows ownership and lifetime from creation through sharing, mutation, cleanup, and failure instead of relying on syntax alone.
keyPoints: Trace allocation and cleanup.
Make aliasing and mutation explicit.
Treat resource lifetime separately from garbage-collected memory where applicable.

theorySections.title: Concurrency and I/O
theorySections.explanation: Concurrency in Hugging Face must be derived from its runtime and host platform. Explain what can execute independently, how work waits, how cancellation and backpressure propagate, and which synchronization rule protects shared invariants.
keyPoints: Distinguish concurrency from parallelism.
State the ordering or synchronization guarantee.
Bound queues, retries, and resource use.

theorySections.title: Production behavior
theorySections.explanation: A production Hugging Face system is evaluated through tests, diagnostics, performance evidence, security boundaries, compatible changes, and recovery. Convenient abstractions are useful only when their hidden cost and failure signals remain observable.
keyPoints: Measure before optimizing.
Validate untrusted boundaries and use least privilege.
Design rollback, migration, and failure diagnosis with the feature.

misconceptions.claim: Hugging Face best practices are universal rules.
misconceptions.correction: Practices are responses to constraints; state the workload, invariant, and trade-off before applying one.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Interview summaries often omit the forces that justify a recommendation.

misconceptions.claim: A successful Hugging Face build proves runtime correctness.
misconceptions.correction: Build-time checks cover only declared contracts; runtime inputs, integration, resource limits, and concurrency still need evidence.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Fast local feedback is confused with end-to-end behavior.

misconceptions.claim: The most concise Hugging Face API is automatically the most efficient.
misconceptions.correction: Abstractions can hide allocation, I/O, network calls, queries, synchronization, or retries; inspect and measure the execution path.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Source-code size is used as a proxy for work performed.

misconceptions.claim: Adding parallelism always speeds up Hugging Face workloads.
misconceptions.correction: Useful parallelism is bounded by dependencies and resources; coordination, contention, queueing, and downstream limits can reduce throughput.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Available threads or workers are mistaken for additional system capacity.
